parts.text: When businesses over order, or make inaccurate predictions about demand, food spoils. And research shows that poor

around production, logistics and sales leads to significant food wastage.

Sleek digital supply chains are designed to fix this problem. Forecasting software (which predicts who needs what and when) and automated ordering mean less food sits in a

going off. That is a real gain, environmentally and economically.

The challenge is that these efficiency improvements can limit the capacity to absorb unforeseen disruption. When stores hold only a few days’ stock and every step

on software, there is little to fall back on when something – a hacker, a flood or a war – cuts off supplies.

The UK government has been warned about this, with the National Audit Office saying that food supply chains have

efficiency, keeping costs down for businesses and shoppers, but leaving them vulnerable to shocks.

So, does improving resilience mean giving up efficiency and returning to massive warehouse stockpiles?

Not

.

After the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted wheat and sunflower oil supplies in 2022, we were part of a team which surveyed over 300 food manufacturers that relied on supplies coming from the region.

Waste not

The firms that coped best did two things. They worked hard to

waste in their processes (by reusing and recycling materials, for example), and they quickly reorganised, finding alternative suppliers.

For supermarkets then, the lesson is to plan for disruption as

as they plan for efficiency. Two changes can be implemented in a short period.

The first is localisation, where sourcing more food from the UK will help shorten supply chains and reduce dependency on distant suppliers and long transport

options: Climate-related risks discourage investment in poorer countries and can also harm corporations.
